title: The Bedroom
short_description: In 1888, Van Gogh moved into his own home in Arles, France. He dubbed it the “Studio of the South,” hoping that fellow artists would join him there to work. This is one of three versions he painted of his beloved Arles bedroom. While its vivid palette and dramatic perspective seem to burst with nervous vitality, Van Gogh intended the painting "to express utter repose."

title: Nightlife
short_description: A native Chicagoan and graduate of the School of the Art Institute, Motley used his art to represent the vibrancy of African American culture, frequently portraying young, sophisticated city dwellers out on the town. One of Motley’s most celebrated paintings, Nightlife depicts a crowded cabaret in the South Side Bronzeville neighborhood. The dynamic composition, intense lighting, and heightened colors vividly express the scene's liveliness.

title: American Gothic
short_description: One of America’s most famous paintings, American Gothic debuted at the Art Institute of Chicago, winning Grant Wood a $300 prize and instant fame. Wood used his sister and dentist as models, depicting them in front of an 1880s-style house. While the painting is often seen as a satirical commentary on the Midwestern character, Wood intended it to a positive statement about rural American values.

title: Sky above Clouds IV
short_description: Painted in the summer of 1965, when Georgia O’Keeffe was 77 years old, this monumental work is the final painting in a series the artist made based on her experiences as an airplane passenger. Because of its size and its status as an icon of the museum's collection, the work has not left the Art Institute since it came into the building in 1983.

title: Woman at Her Toilette
short_description: Rendered with feathery brushstrokes in shades of lavender, pink, blue, white, and gray, this Impressionist painting captures a subject often explored by male artists of the day but seldom broached by the period's few women artists. Morisot presents a decidely female perspective, intimate yet not eroticized. She signed her name along the bottom of the mirror, as if to suggest that the image in her painting is as ephemeral as a silvery reﬂection.

title: The Beach at Sainte-Adresse
short_description: In 1867 Monet stayed with his aunt in Sainte-Adresse, a suburb of the port city of Le Havre in Normandy, where the artist grew up. Monet began the painting outdoors but likely revised it in his studio. Technical analysis of the work revealed that it started as a beach scene of yachts and tourists but ultimately became a view of sailboats and local fishermen.

title: Cupid Chastised
short_description: This dramatic scene by Bartolomeo Manfredi shows Mars, the god of war, beating Cupid for having caused his affair with Venus, the goddess of love. The sheer physicality of the figures as well as the bold illumination from the left further the work's dynamism. The composition is on one level a tale of domestic disturbance but also symbolizes the eternal conflict between love and war.

title: Acrobats at the Cirque Fernando (Francisca and Angelina Wartenberg)
short_description: The two girls in this painting by Pierre-Auguste Renoir are Francisca and Angelina Wartenberg, acrobats who performed in the famed Cirque Fernando in Paris. They are depicted clutching oranges tossed to them from the crowd as gifts. Although they are painted standing in the center of a circus ring, Renoir actually painted them in his studio, where he could take full advantage of natural sunlight.

title: Little Harbor in Normandy
short_description: This work is the first fully realized example of Georges Braque’s early Cubist style. He described the English Channel coast in severe geometries and a sober palette, reduced in range and intensity to pale shades of color. His compressed treatment of space and use of a shifting perspective seem to propel the two sailboats forward to the front edges of the picture.

title: The Annunciation
artist_display: Jean Hey (Master of Moulins; Netherlandish, c. 1480-c.1504)
short_description: Jean Hey, known as the Master of Moulins, was a leading painter in 15th-century France. Here, he captured the moment the archangel Gabriel announced to Mary that she would give birth to a son. The painting once formed the right side of an altarpiece, with the left side depicting Mary’s own Immaculate Conception and a central section, now lost, featuring the enthroned Virgin and Child.

title: Portrait Vessel
artist_display:
Ceramist unknown (Moche)
Southern Moche region, north coast, Peru
short_description: Ceramic portrait vessels produced by artists of the Moche culture are the only discernible examples of portraiture, in a Euro-American sense, from the ancient Andes. Vessels like this one were often placed in burials as funerary offerings. They may also have been sent as emblems of royal authority, or even emissaries, to other elite individuals in nearby settlements.

title: Henri Degas and His Niece Lucie Degas (The Artist's Uncle and Cousin)
short_description: Perhaps the most subtle portrait painter in the Impressionist group, Edgar Degas painted this double portrait in the mid-1970s. It shows his orphaned first cousin, Lucie, and their uncle Henri, in whose care the girl had recently been placed—two people who are tentatively accepting the circumstances of their new relationship. Having recently lost his own father, Degas addressed his subjects with awareness and sensitivity.

title: Spoon Woman
short_description: Evoking a female body through simplified shapes that suggest a head, shoulders, chest, and a wide, concave womb, this sculpture was inspired by a ceremonial ladle created by the Dan communities of Liberia and Côte d’Ivoire. Giacometti appreciated these objects, known as a wakemia or wunkirmian, for their geometry and literal rendering of bodily volumes—an alternative approach to Western modes of modeling and carving.

title: Adam
short_description: Auguste Rodin's figure of Adam was originally intended to be paired with a sculpture of Eve to flank his monumental bronze portal, The Gates of Hell, for the Musée de Arts Décoratifs, Paris. Rodin created over 200 of its figures and groupings, exploring the expressive potential of the human body. However, the museum building was never constructed and the portal never completed as originally conceived.

title: The Combat of the Giaour and Hassan
short_description: This colorful scene was inspired by a poem from Lord Byron’s “oriental tales,” a popular series of romances. Both the poem and painting are examples of 19th-century Europeans’ interest in fantastical and often violent depictions of Middle Eastern, North African, and Asian cultures, which reinforced colonialist aims. Delacroix began painting Orientalist subjects early in his career, though he did not visit North Africa until 1832.

title: Movement
short_description: Unlike many American artists, Marsden Hartley was more drawn to German Expressionism than to French modernism. This painting, made in Berlin, possesses an energy that evokes both the vibrancy of modern Berlin and movements of music. Like the painter Vasily Kandinsky, Hartley sought to make his work more like music, which he admired for its potential to be purely spiritual and separate from material reality.

title: Reliquary Casket of Saints Adrian and Natalia
short_description: This rare casket, fashioned like a miniature tomb complete with Romanesque columns, was made to contain the relics of Saint Adrian, patron saint of soldiers and protector against the plague. A Roman officer charged with persecuting Christians, Adrian so admired the virtues of those he oppressed that he converted. After declaring himself a Christian, Adrian was arrested and brutally martyred in the early fourth century.

title: Lion (One of a Pair, South Pedestal)
artist_display:
Edward Kemeys (American, 1843–1907)
American Bronze Founding Company (American, founded 1886)
Chicago
short_description: Iconic guardians of the museum, Edward Kemeys's bronze lions have stood on Michigan Avenue since 1894. An essentially self-taught artist and the nation’s first great animalier (sculptor of animals), Kemeys chose for the Art Institute larger-than-life African lions; the one north of the steps is “on the prowl,” while the one to the south is “in an attitude of defiance."

title: Water Lily Pond
short_description: In 1893, Claude Monet began transforming the marshy ground behind his Giverny home into a pond, on the narrow end of which he built a Japanese-style wood bridge. Adding both exotic and domestic plantings, including his famous water lilies, the artist created the garden that would be one of his principal subjects for the rest of his life.

title: Kantharos (Wine Cup)
artist_display:
Greek; Apulia, Italy 
probably made in Canosa, said to have been found in Tarento, Italy
short_description: This is an example of one of the most popular types of wine cup in ancient Greece, the kantharos. Rising from a round foot and a thin stem, the cup flares out to a wide bowl with two handles on opposite sides. While most examples are glazed, this elegant exception bears evidence it was once gilded. Before firing it was also inscribed with the word "Aphrodites" near the lip of the cup.
department_title: Arts of Greece, Rome, and Byzantium

title: The Banquet
short_description: This canvas by René Magritte is the last and largest of four paintings with this title, each a slightly different outdoor scene with a sun superimposed atop dark trees. The compositions create a visual conundrum, with the sun fully visible when it should be hidden by the trees. Here, the darkening landscape framing the sun's deep-red glow further dramatizes the picture's "charge of strangeness."

artist_display:

title: Poppy Field (Giverny)
short_description: In July 1890, Claude Monet began four almost identically scaled canvases showing poppy fields near his home in Giverny. Although he did not consider these to be a series, like the 25 paintings of stacks of wheat that he began that same summer, the works certainly show his growing interest in developing several canvases simultaneously. They also demonstrate more uniform brushwork than his earlier landscapes.

artist_display:

title: Desert Forms
short_description: Hughie Lee-Smith here conjures an unsettling scene. Anonymous figures, disconnected from one another, face away from the viewer amid austere terrain. The artist often placed enigmatic people in bleak landscapes, aligning these visualizations with his experiences as an African American: “Unconsciously it has a lot to do with a sense of alienation . . . and in all Blacks there is an awareness of their isolation from the mainstream of society.”

title: Fish Plate
short_description: This skillfully decorated Athenian plate was made to serve the sea life it depicts. A scallop sits between a gilt-head bream and a red mullet. Opposite them, a lettered perch confronts a spiny scorpion fish. Shells, a small fish, and a mollusk or crustacean ring the outside. The central cavity, decorated with wave patterns, would have collected the delicious juices from the cooked fish.
department_title: Arts of Greece, Rome, and Byzantium

title: Vétheuil
short_description: In the summer of 1901, Claude Monet rented a home across the Seine from Vétheuil and not far from his property at Giverny. From the balcony of his rental he began 15 paintings of Vétheuil, all of which feature the same view of the riverbank and town—punctuated by the church—and document the changes in light throughout the day. The Art Institute holds two paintings from this series, one from midday and another from sunset.

title: Rinaldo and the Magus of Ascalon
short_description: The fourth and final large narrative canvas from Giovanni Battista Tiepolo’s decorative Rinaldo and Armida suite takes place as Rinaldo rejoins the crusader army. The magician of Ascalon uses Rinaldo’s shield to conjure the heroic deeds of his ancestors and urge him to live up to their legacy. In his choice to return to battle, Rinaldo would have served as a positive example of civic duty for the family who commissioned these decorations.

title: The Music Lesson
short_description: One of Ochtervelt’s finest works, The Music Lesson was probably painted in Rotterdam, where the artist spent most of his career. The delicate light, which illuminates the girl and leaves the youth partly in shadow, is indebted to Johannes Vermeer, who worked in the nearby city of Delft. Characteristic of Ochtervelt, however, are the angled poses and the playful interchange between the figures.

title: Cattle at Rest on a Hillside in the Alps
Landscape with the Penitent Saint Jerome
Canopic Jar of Amenhotep
date_display: New Kingdom, Dynasty 18, reign of Amenhotep II (about 1427–1400 BCE)
artist_display: Egyptian; Tomb A7, Dra Abu el-Naga, Thebes (now Luxor), Egypt
short_description: This now-empty jar is one of four that once held the liver, lungs, intestines, and stomach of Amenhotep, the overseer of architectural projects in the temple of Amun at Karnak (in present-day Luxor). Each jar has a hand-sculpted stopper that may represent its owner or one of the sons of Horus, gods associated with these organs. An inscription in hieroglyphs on each container promises divine protection from a different goddess over its contents.
